reader: AI reader 33 (targeted check at the stated place, PDFs)

results.note: Every number matches. p. 2, 2.1, 1st paragraph (starts at the foot of the left column, continues in the right): MATES of 400 people entering community-based treatment in Sydney and Brisbane and 101 people in Sydney not in treatment (needle and syringe programmes, outreach), recruited 2006 and 2007, follow-up interviews 2006 to 2010; 2nd paragraph: 469 analysed, 379, 357 and 315 interviewed at 3 months, 12 months and 3 years, 1518 months of data for property crime, fraud and violent crime. 2.1.1.1: violent crime is any crime involving violence, such as violence in a robbery or assault, on the OTI crime scale. Table 1 (p. 3, rendered page): 19 (3%) of 593 and 113 (12%) of 927 months; 8.2 (4.2–15.9); Model 1 5.3 (printed '5.3.', 2.6–10.7); Model 2 3.4 (1.5–8.0), p 0.005. Table 1 notes a and b and 2.1.2 give the covariates (age, income, unemployment, unstable accommodation; alcohol and cannabis as 0, 1–15 and 16+ days; any cocaine, heroin and ecstasy). 3.2, 1st and 2nd paragraphs: the unadjusted and adjusted results in words. '469 people with DSM-IV dependence at entry' is right for the analysed sample (484 met the criterion before the other two exclusions; card reporting issue 5). Role supports: right for the statement's adjusted association in the dependent cohort.

Every element is at the stated places. 2.1.2 (p. 3): exploratory and not pre-registered; random-effects logit models (xtlogit) with a random intercept, and the fixed-effects option used for the within-person effect; the covariates include neither treatment, imprisonment nor tobacco (tobacco days were recorded, 2.1.1.2). 3.1, 2nd paragraph: use in 61% of observed months, median 10 days (IQR 3–20), injection the main route in 80%. 3.2, 3rd paragraph (p. 3, ending on p. 4) and Fig. 1: unadjusted percentages by no use, 1–15 and 16+ days; the adjusted dose relation is referred to Table S3 only. 4.1, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 5): self-reported crime, not convictions; the direction of the same-month relationship open to dispute; few participants committing crime when not using, hence large confidence limits; small numbers limit the dose findings; dependent and mostly injecting, not to be generalised to recreational use. Fig. 1 measured independently on a 300-dpi rendering against its gridlines: violent crime 3.2%, 9.3% and 19.2%, so 'about 3%, 9% and 19%' is right. The no-use bars reproduce Table 1's shares of months, so 'of months' is right although the caption says 'percentage of participants'. No count of contributing participants appears anywhere in the paper. Role qualifies: right.

Abstract, Conclusions (p. 1): significant increases in crime beyond premorbid risk; crime a likely social consequence of use. Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 4): 'robust evidence' of a large increase; 3rd paragraph: violent crime not only a consequence of pre-existing risk, and instrumental (robbery) and expressive (domestic assault) violence cannot be told apart. Introduction, 3rd paragraph (p. 2): the same within-person approach applied earlier to hostility and psychotic symptoms (2013b, 2014). Introduction, 1st paragraph (p. 1) cites both McKetin et al. (2019) and Foulds et al. (2020). Author list (p. 1) against the reference list (p. 6): Foulds et al. (2020) is Foulds, Boden, McKetin and Newton-Howes, so three of four are authors here; McKetin et al. (2019) includes McKetin, Foulds, Farrell and Degenhardt, so four. Role qualifies: right.

All on SOM p. 2 (p. 1 is the unnumbered cover; printed page numbers equal the PDF pages), Study sample, 1st to 3rd paragraphs. 1st: East Anglia, advertisements and treatment services, Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV; same biological parents; one sibling with DSM-IV-TR cocaine or amphetamine dependence; the other without personal history of substance dependence except nicotine; controls without personal or family history of drug or alcohol dependence; aged 18–55. 2nd: 154 enrolled, 150 completed in three groups of 50; scans unavailable for three dependent participants and one sibling, leaving 47, 49 and 50. 3rd: 94% cocaine and 6% amphetamines; 16.3 (±7.6) years of use from 16.5 (±2.8); urine positive except three samples; another dependence in the majority (opiates 55%, alcohol 26%, cannabis 9%); siblings' and controls' drug experience minor by very low DAST and AUDIT scores; their urine drug-negative. A text search finds no 'methamphetamine' in the supplement or the report. Role qualifies: right.

Table S1 (SOM p. 8, rendered page) matches every value: men 64%, 51% and 92%, chi-square 19.0, P < 0.001; age 32.8, 32.6 and 34.5, P = 0.702; NART 112.3, 108.9 and 110.3, P = 0.143; education 12.6, 12.1 and 11.6, P = 0.062; current smokers 12%, 55% and 94%, 71.8; shared upbringing 90% and 92% to age 10, 75% and 89% to age 15; AUDIT 3.3, 3.9 and 11.4; DAST-20 0.0 and 0.5, with '--' for the dependent group. SOM p. 3: the 5th paragraph gives t(70.9) = −0.72, P = 0.472, and says participants were not breathalysed; Statistical analysis: gender a covariate in all analyses of demographics and stop-signal performance; the 4th paragraph (p. 2, continuing on p. 3): the dependent participants were still using, not asked to withdraw, screened for intoxication sufficient to incapacitate. Role qualifies: right. Optional addition: Table S1 gives the DAST-20 comparison as F 12.6, P 0.001, so the non-dependent siblings scored significantly higher than the controls, although both scores are very low.

SOM p. 4, MRI data processing and analyses: 146 participants (50, 47, 49); CamBA permutation testing thresholded at one error cluster per image, P = 9 × 10⁻⁴ (controls against siblings) and 8 × 10⁻⁴ (controls against dependent participants); four and eight clusters; the voxels surviving the intersection lie in three regions; single-sex comparisons did not change the results. DTI, 1st paragraph (p. 4, continuing on p. 5): 145 participants (50, 46, 49), one dependent participant unable to tolerate the full session; 2nd paragraph (p. 5): permutation F and t tests, threshold-free cluster enhancement, 5000 permutations, corrected at P < 0.05, mean thresholded skeleton values taken to SPSS. Table S2 (p. 9, rendered page): 24,934 voxels, 0.55, 0.53 and 0.52 (±0.02); amygdala L 984 mm³, 0.76, 0.81 and 0.83 (±0.07); putamen L 560 mm³, 0.34 (±0.05), 0.38 (±0.06), 0.38 (±0.05); postcentral gyrus L 1,152 mm³, 0.89 (±0.12), 0.75 (±0.11), 0.74 (±0.11); the caption says the values are for voxels that differed significantly between groups. Editors' calculation recomputed with n-weighted pooled SDs: 0.71, 0.72 and 1.22 (siblings) and 1.00, 0.80 and 1.30 (dependent participants), so the rounded values stand. Role supports: right.

SOM p. 5, Assessment of familiality: variance of within-pair differences against 100,000 random re-pairings of each dependent participant with an unrelated sibling, compared with the 5000th value for a one-tailed test at P < 0.05; no covariates described. Tobacco section: 1st paragraph (p. 5, continuing on p. 6) gives 12%, 55% and 94% smokers, the literature's regions (prefrontal cortex, cingulate gyrus, anterior insula; Table S3) and the label amygdala/hippocampus; 2nd paragraph (p. 6): re-analysis of non-smoking controls and siblings, amygdala, putamen and postcentral gyrus still significant, no numbers or statistics, followed by the sentence saying the differences might instead be due to tobacco; 3rd paragraph: smoking as part of the siblings' genetic risk. Fig. S1 legend (p. 6) and Table S2 say amygdala; Table S3 (p. 10) says amygdala/hippocampus at −22, −6, −16. No smoking analysis of FA or the stop-signal task anywhere, though the heading names white matter. Fig. S2 legend (p. 7): FA negatively correlated with years of stimulant use, less extensive than the familial effect; grey matter negatively correlated with duration, distinctly different from the endophenotype effects; no statistics, names, threshold or age adjustment. 'Orbitofrontal' occurs nowhere, and the anterior insula appears only as a tobacco region from earlier studies (p. 5), so 'names no orbitofrontal or anterior insular cluster' is right. Role qualifies: right.

note: Sources: McKetin et al. (2020), PDF pp. 1–6, and the Supporting Online Material of Ersche et al. (2012), 12 pages, both read in full (the main report, pp. 601–604, read for context). Text extracted with pdftotext -layout; Table 1, Fig. 1, Tables S1–S3 and Figs. S1–S2 checked on pages rendered at 110 dpi, and Fig. 1's bars measured at 300 dpi. A mechanical search found every number of two or more digits in the seven anchors on the stated pages, except the editors' standardized differences in anchor 6, which I recomputed. I wrote none of these anchors and none of the card findings they match.
